context: Current closing price of Nasdaq Inc (NDAQ): $91.98 USD as of 2026-05-19.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly upward-drifting baseline assumption across the three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 92.5 is anchored closely to what I would have assumed was the prevailing market or index level at the time, with only modest drift expected over such a short window. The slight upward trajectory from 92.5 to 93.2 at one week and 94.5 at one month reflects a gentle positive drift assumption, consistent with long-run equity risk premium logic or mean-reversion toward a modestly higher fundamental value. I was essentially assuming no major catalysts in the near term and projecting a continuation of recent trend with a small positive bias.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a direct reflection of the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty under standard random walk assumptions. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 6 points (89.5 to 95.5), which implies relatively low realized volatility expectations over a single session. By one month, the interval has expanded to 23 points (83.0 to 106.0), capturing the compounding of daily uncertainty over roughly 20 trading days. The asymmetric widening on both sides also reflects fat-tail concerns — markets tend to exhibit non-normal distributions with heavier downside tails, so the lower bound was set somewhat conservatively.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant credit event in the financial system. On the upside, a surprise positive earnings season, a major policy stimulus announcement, or a rapid de-escalation of existing geopolitical tensions could propel prices well above the upper bound of my one-month interval. Liquidity crises or flash crash dynamics could also cause intraday moves that breach even my one-day interval.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes. If implied volatility were to spike — as it does during risk-off episodes — the actual distribution of outcomes would be much wider than what I modeled. My estimates were fundamentally backward-looking in their volatility assumptions, which is a known limitation. A regime change in volatility alone, independent of any directional move, could render my stated confidence intervals too narrow even if the point estimates remain reasonable.
